intro: Most Buddhists in the world today read texts that are not in the Pali Canon. In East Asia, people chant the Heart Sutra, honor the Lotus Sutra and call the name of Amitabha Buddha. In Tibet, monks study huge collections of translated texts and sing the songs of great yogis. In this unit, you will explore Mahayana sutras, Zen writings and Tibetan texts.

You will read the parable of the burning house, meet the bodhisattva of compassion, and learn what Mahayana teachers mean by emptiness. Then you will look at Zen koans and the Platform Sutra, Dogen's writings, Milarepa's life, the so-called Tibetan Book of the Dead and Shantideva's poem.

By the end, you will be able to explain key ideas like skillful means, emptiness and the bodhisattva path, tell how different schools choose their central texts, and show how a text's meaning can change when it reaches new readers.
bigQuestion: How do Mahayana, Zen and Tibetan Buddhists use their texts, and how have outsiders read them?

title: Mahayana Sutras, Zen and Tibet

chapters.title: The Lotus Sutra and the Heart Sutra
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Mahayana sutras use parables, short chants and new figures to teach, and why do Mahayana Buddhists treasure them?

story.title: Carts Full of Toys
story.kicker: A father must get his children out of a burning house, but they are too busy playing to listen.
paragraphs: Chapter 3 of the Lotus Sutra tells a parable. A rich old man owns a large, crumbling house with only one door. One day, fire breaks out. Inside, his children are playing games. They do not know what fire is, and they do not want to stop playing.

The father calls to them to come out, but they ignore him. He thinks quickly. He knows what they love. So he shouts that outside the door are carts they have always wanted: carts pulled by goats, by deer and by oxen.

The children rush out, pushing each other through the door, and they are safe. Then the father gives each child not the small carts he promised, but one great, splendid cart pulled by a white ox, better than anything they imagined.

In the sutra, the Buddha then asks: did the father lie? His disciple Sariputra answers no, because he saved his children's lives. Mahayana Buddhists read the story as a picture of how the Buddha teaches: using many methods to lead beings out of suffering toward one great goal.
story.think: Was the father right to promise something different from what he gave? Why or why not?

lessons.title: Where Mahayana Sutras Came From
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars date Mahayana sutras from about the 1st century BCE onward; Mahayana Buddhists see them as the Buddha's word.
reading: Around the 1st century BCE and after, new Buddhist sutras began to circulate in India. They were written in Sanskrit and related languages. They called themselves the words of the Buddha and opened with 'Thus have I heard,' like the older suttas.

Modern scholars date these *Mahayana sutras* by their language, ideas and first translations into Chinese. Many were written down over several centuries. Scholars see them as a new wave of Buddhist writing.

Mahayana Buddhists understand them differently. Some traditions teach that the Buddha taught these sutras to those ready to hear them, and that they were kept hidden until the time was right. Others stress that they express the Buddha's true meaning. For them the sutras carry full *authority*.

words.d: scriptures of Mahayana Buddhism, in Sanskrit and later Chinese and Tibetan
the reason a community trusts and follows a text
Sanskrit for a Buddhist scripture or talk (Pali: sutta)

look.title: Two Ways to Date a Sutra
look.text: A historian says: the Lotus Sutra was likely composed in India between about 100 BCE and 200 CE, based on its language and its first Chinese translation in 286 CE. A Nichiren Buddhist says: the Lotus Sutra is the Buddha's highest teaching, given near the end of his life.
look.prompt: What kind of evidence does each speaker use? Can both be described fairly?

check.q: About when do scholars say Mahayana sutras began to circulate?
check.why: Scholars date them from roughly the 1st century BCE onward.

check.q: How do many Mahayana Buddhists understand these sutras?

check.why: Mahayana traditions treat them as authoritative teachings of the Buddha.

check.q: What evidence do scholars use to date a sutra?
choices: Only the sutra's own opening line
check.why: Dating relies on language and the dates of translations.

lessons.title: The Lotus Sutra
lessons.mainIdea: The Lotus Sutra teaches that all beings can become buddhas and is central in East Asian Buddhism.
reading: The *Lotus Sutra* (Saddharma Pundarika Sutra, 'Sutra of the Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most important Mahayana texts. Its best-known Chinese translation was made by Kumarajiva in 406 CE.

The sutra teaches that the different paths the Buddha taught are really one path, the 'one vehicle', leading to buddhahood. It says that all beings, even those who seem far from it, can become buddhas.

In East Asia, the Lotus Sutra shaped the Tiantai school in China and the Tendai school in Japan. The Japanese teacher Nichiren (1222–1282) taught that chanting its title is the heart of practice. Nichiren Buddhists today, including Soka Gakkai members, continue this practice. The lotus itself is a *symbol*.

words.d: a major Mahayana sutra teaching the one vehicle and the buddhahood of all beings
the Lotus Sutra's teaching that all Buddhist paths lead to one goal, buddhahood
a thing that stands for an idea; the lotus grows clean from muddy water

look.title: Lotus Sutra Milestones
look.cite: Standard reference dates for the Lotus Sutra and Nichiren
look.prompt: How many years after Kumarajiva's translation was Nichiren born?

check.q: Who made the best-known Chinese translation of the Lotus Sutra?
check.why: Kumarajiva translated it in 406 CE.

check.q: What does the 'one vehicle' teaching say?
choices: All Buddhist paths lead to one goal, buddhahood
There are three separate goals forever
check.why: The Lotus Sutra teaches one vehicle to buddhahood.

check.q: Which Japanese teacher centered practice on chanting the Lotus Sutra's title?
check.why: Nichiren taught chanting the sutra's title.

lessons.title: Skillful Means
lessons.mainIdea: The Lotus Sutra's idea of skillful means says the Buddha adapts his teaching to each listener.
reading: Chapter 2 of the Lotus Sutra is titled 'Skillful Means' (Sanskrit *upaya*). It says the Buddha, as the sutra presents him, adjusts his teaching to what each listener can understand, like a good teacher or doctor.
The burning house parable in Chapter 3 shows this idea. The father's promise of three carts is a skillful means to get the children out; the one great cart stands for the one vehicle.

Mahayana readers have used skillful means to explain why the Buddha seems to teach different things in different texts. Critics within and outside Buddhism have asked where skillful means ends and misleading begins. The sutra's own answer is that the father's *intention* was to save his children.

words.d: upaya; adapting a teaching to what a listener can understand
a short story that teaches a lesson by comparison
the purpose behind an action

look.title: The Burning House
look.text: The father, seeing his children absorbed in play inside the burning house, knows they will not heed a warning. So he tells them that the carts they love are waiting outside. Once they are safe, he gives each one a great cart drawn by a white ox.
look.cite: Lotus Sutra, ch. 3 (Parable); see Burton Watson, The Lotus Sutra (1993), from Kumarajiva's Chinese (406 CE)
look.prompt: In the parable, who stands for the Buddha, and who stands for ordinary beings?

check.q: What is skillful means?
choices: Adapting a teaching to what a listener can understand
check.why: Upaya means adapting a teaching to the listener.

check.q: In the parable, what does the one great cart stand for?
check.why: The great cart represents the single goal.

check.q: What question have critics asked about skillful means?
choices: Where it ends and misleading begins
Whether the sutra is in Pali
check.why: The parable raises a question about truth-telling.

lessons.title: The Heart Sutra
lessons.mainIdea: The Heart Sutra is a very short Mahayana text on emptiness, chanted daily in much of East Asia.
reading: The *Heart Sutra* is one of the shortest Buddhist sutras. The common Chinese version has about 260 characters. It belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom (prajnaparamita) family of sutras.
In it, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara speaks to Shariputra about *emptiness* (Sanskrit shunyata). Its most famous lines say that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. It ends with a short mantra.
Monks, nuns and laypeople in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam chant the Heart Sutra daily. It is often copied by hand as a practice. Many Zen, Chan and Pure Land temples include it in services.

words.d: a very short Mahayana sutra on emptiness, widely chanted in East Asia
shunyata; the Mahayana teaching that nothing exists on its own, apart from causes and conditions
a short sacred phrase that is chanted or repeated

look.title: Form and Emptiness
look.text: Avalokiteshvara tells Shariputra that form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; the same is true of feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness.
look.cite: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita Hrdaya), Chinese version attributed to Xuanzang (649 CE); see Red Pine, The Heart Sutra (2004)
look.prompt: What pattern do you notice in the list of five items? Where have you seen it before?

check.q: About how many characters is the common Chinese Heart Sutra?
check.why: It is famously short, about 260 characters.

check.q: Who speaks in the Heart Sutra?
check.why: The bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara addresses Shariputra.

check.q: What is emptiness in Mahayana teaching?
choices: Nothing exists on its own, apart from causes and conditions
check.why: Shunyata means lacking independent existence.

lessons.title: What Emptiness Means
lessons.mainIdea: Mahayana teachers explain emptiness as the idea that things depend on causes and conditions.
reading: Emptiness is easy to misunderstand. Mahayana teachers stress that it does not mean nothing exists. Rather, they teach that nothing has a fixed, separate self. Everything depends on other things.

The Indian philosopher Nagarjuna (c. 2nd century CE) developed this idea in his *Madhyamaka*, or 'middle way', school. He linked emptiness to the older teaching of dependent arising, found in the Pali suttas.

Teachers often use everyday examples. A table depends on wood, a carpenter, rain that grew the tree and much more. Mahayana Buddhists say seeing this *interdependence* clearly weakens grasping and brings freedom.

words.d: the 'middle way' school of Mahayana philosophy founded by Nagarjuna
the way everything depends on other things

look.title: A Sheet of Paper
look.text: A teacher holds up a sheet of paper. She asks: what made it? A tree. What made the tree grow? Sun, rain, soil. Who cut it? A logger, who ate bread made from wheat. The teacher says Mahayana Buddhists see the paper as 'empty' of a separate self in this sense.
look.prompt: How does this example show interdependence? What does it not say?

check.q: Do Mahayana teachers say emptiness means nothing exists?
choices: No; they say nothing has a fixed, separate self
check.why: Emptiness means lacking independent existence, not nonexistence.

check.q: Who founded the Madhyamaka school?
check.why: Nagarjuna (c. 2nd century CE) developed Madhyamaka.

check.q: Which older teaching did Nagarjuna link to emptiness?
check.why: He connected emptiness to dependent arising from the suttas.

lessons.title: Chanting the Heart Sutra
lessons.mainIdea: In East Asia the Heart Sutra is chanted, copied and treasured in daily Buddhist life.
reading: In many Japanese Zen and Korean temples, the Heart Sutra is chanted at morning services. A wooden drum shaped like a fish, called a *moktak* in Korean or mokugyo in Japanese, keeps the beat.
Copying the sutra by hand, called *shakyo* in Japanese, is another practice. People trace or write each character carefully with a brush. Temples often receive these copies as offerings.
For many East Asian Buddhists, the sutra is valued both for its meaning and as a sacred text in itself. Its closing mantra is chanted in a form close to the Sanskrit sound rather than translated.

words.d: a wooden fish-shaped drum used to keep time in chanting (Japanese: mokugyo)
the Japanese practice of copying sutras by hand

look.title: A Morning Service
look.text: Before dawn in a Korean mountain temple, a nun strikes a wooden fish drum. Monks and nuns in gray robes chant the Heart Sutra together, fast and steady, in Korean-pronounced Chinese. The chant ends with the short mantra.
look.prompt: Why might a community chant a text in an older form rather than in everyday speech?

check.q: What is shakyo?
check.why: Shakyo is hand-copying sutras in Japan.

check.q: What keeps the beat in many chanting services?
check.why: The moktak or mokugyo marks the rhythm.

check.q: How is the Heart Sutra's closing mantra usually chanted?
choices: In a form close to its Sanskrit sound
check.why: The mantra keeps a sound close to Sanskrit.

lessons.title: Avalokiteshvara and Guanyin
lessons.mainIdea: Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, is honored across Asia under many names.
reading: *Avalokiteshvara* is the bodhisattva of compassion. The name is often explained as 'the lord who looks down' on the world with care. Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sutra says that those in danger who call his name will be helped.

In China, Avalokiteshvara became *Guanyin*, 'one who perceives the cries of the world'. Over the centuries, Guanyin came to be shown mostly as a woman in white. In Japan the name is Kannon, in Korea Gwaneum and in Vietnam Quan Am.

Tibetan Buddhists call this bodhisattva Chenrezig and believe the Dalai Lama is his emanation. Many Buddhists pray to Avalokiteshvara for help, and statues of Guanyin stand in Chinese and Vietnamese temples in Chicago.

words.d: the bodhisattva of compassion in Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism
the Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara, often shown as a woman in white
caring about the suffering of others and wishing to help

look.title: The Universal Gate
look.text: The sutra says that if people caught in fire, flood, shipwreck or danger call the name of the bodhisattva who perceives the world's sounds with one mind, they will be rescued.
look.cite: Lotus Sutra, ch. 25 (Universal Gate of Avalokiteshvara); see Burton Watson, The Lotus Sutra (1993)
look.prompt: Why might this chapter have become so popular among ordinary people?

check.q: What is Avalokiteshvara the bodhisattva of?
check.why: Avalokiteshvara embodies compassion.

check.q: What is Avalokiteshvara called in China?
check.why: Guanyin is the Chinese name.

check.q: Which Lotus Sutra chapter is devoted to Avalokiteshvara?
check.why: Chapter 25 is the Universal Gate chapter.

lessons.title: Amitabha and the Pure Land
lessons.mainIdea: Pure Land sutras describe Amitabha Buddha's land of bliss, and devotees call his name to be reborn there.
reading: The Pure Land sutras describe *Amitabha* Buddha ('Infinite Light'). In the Larger Pure Land Sutra, a monk named Dharmakara makes vows, including a vow that all who sincerely call his name will be reborn in his land. He becomes Amitabha.
His land, *Sukhavati* ('Land of Bliss'), is described with jeweled trees, lotus ponds and birds that sing the teaching. Pure Land Buddhists believe that being born there makes awakening easy.

Pure Land Buddhism is one of the largest forms of Buddhism in East Asia. In China and Vietnam, devotees chant 'Namo Amituofo'. In Japan, Honen and Shinran taught the nembutsu, 'Namu Amida Butsu'. Shinran's Jodo Shinshu is the tradition of the Buddhist Temple of Chicago.

words.d: the Buddha of Infinite Light, center of Pure Land Buddhism (Japanese: Amida)
'Land of Bliss', Amitabha's Pure Land
calling Amida Buddha's name: 'Namu Amida Butsu'

look.title: Dharmakara's Vow
look.text: Dharmakara vows that if, after he becomes a buddha, beings who sincerely trust him and call his name even ten times are not born in his land, he will not accept final awakening.
look.cite: Larger Sukhavativyuha Sutra, 18th vow; see Luis Gómez, The Land of Bliss (1996)
look.prompt: Why is this vow so important to Pure Land Buddhists?

check.q: What does Amitabha mean?
check.why: Amitabha means Infinite Light.

check.q: What is the nembutsu?
check.why: Nembutsu is 'Namu Amida Butsu'.

check.q: Which tradition does the Buddhist Temple of Chicago belong to?
check.why: It is a Shin (Jodo Shinshu) temple.

lessons.title: Many Sutras, Many Paths
lessons.mainIdea: Different Mahayana schools center on different sutras and practices, and each explains its choice.
reading: Mahayana Buddhism has thousands of sutras, and no school uses them all equally. Nichiren Buddhists center the Lotus Sutra. Pure Land Buddhists center the Pure Land sutras. Zen teachers often cite the Heart Sutra and the Diamond Sutra.
Chinese teachers developed ways to sort the sutras, called *doctrinal classification*. The Tiantai school, for example, placed the Lotus Sutra as the Buddha's final and fullest teaching.

From the outside, scholars see how each school's choice of sutras shapes its practice. From the inside, each school explains its choice from its own texts. A fair *comparison* describes these reasons without ranking.

words.d: a Chinese Buddhist method for ordering the sutras by depth or time
looking at how two or more things are alike and different

look.title: Schools and Their Central Sutras
look.cite: Standard descriptions of the Lotus Sutra (Kumarajiva), the three Pure Land sutras and the Heart Sutra
look.prompt: What does the size of each text suggest about how it is used?

check.q: Which sutra is central for Nichiren Buddhists?
check.why: Nichiren centered the Lotus Sutra.

check.q: What is doctrinal classification?
choices: A way to order sutras by depth or time
check.why: Chinese schools used it to rank and sort sutras.

check.q: How does a fair comparison treat different schools?
choices: It describes their reasons without ranking

check.why: Scholars describe each school on its own terms.

choices: The Buddha adapts teaching to listeners

review.why: It teaches that form is emptiness.

chapters.title: Zen Stories and Tibetan Texts
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Zen and Tibetan Buddhists use texts, and what is lost when their words are borrowed by popular culture?

story.title: A Cup That Overflows
story.kicker: A teacher pours tea into a full cup until it spills across the table.
paragraphs: A modern collection of Zen stories, Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (1957), retells a short anecdote. A university professor comes to visit a Japanese Zen master named Nan-in. He wants to learn about Zen. Nan-in lived in Japan in the Meiji era.

Nan-in serves tea. He pours into the professor's cup until it is full, and then he keeps pouring. Tea spills over the rim, across the saucer and onto the table. The professor watches, then cannot stay quiet. "It is full!" he says. "No more will go in!"

"Like this cup," Nan-in says, as the story tells it, "you are full of your own opinions. How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup?" The story ends there, with no further explanation. The professor is left to think.

The story is short, sharp and a little surprising, like many Zen tales. It was collected and retold in English in the 20th century. Readers use it to think about how hard it is to learn something new when we already think we know.
story.think: What might it mean to 'empty your cup' before learning something new?

lessons.title: From Chan to Zen
lessons.mainIdea: Chan Buddhism grew in China, spread to Korea, Vietnam and Japan, and stresses meditation and direct insight.
reading: *Chan* Buddhism took shape in China from about the 6th to 8th centuries CE. The word chan comes from the Sanskrit dhyana, meaning meditation. In Japan it is called Zen, in Korea Seon and in Vietnam Thien.

Chan tradition traces itself to Bodhidharma, an Indian monk who, the tradition says, came to China around 500 CE. Later sources give Chan a famous saying: 'a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words'.

Yet Chan and Zen produced huge numbers of texts: sermons, records of teachers and collections of encounters. Scholars note this *paradox*: a tradition that says it does not depend on words has created a rich literature. Its heart is *transmission* from teacher to student.

words.d: a school of Buddhism that grew in China, stressing meditation; Zen in Japan
something that seems to contradict itself but may still be true
passing a teaching from teacher to student

look.title: Names for the Same Tradition
look.cite: Standard histories of Chan, Seon and Zen; dates rounded
look.prompt: In what order did the tradition reach these three countries?

check.q: What does 'chan' come from?
check.why: Chan and Zen both come from dhyana.

check.q: Whom does Chan tradition name as its founder in China?
check.why: Tradition says Bodhidharma came to China around 500 CE.

check.q: What paradox do scholars note about Zen?
choices: It says it does not depend on words yet produced many texts
check.why: Zen literature is vast despite its saying about words.

lessons.title: The Platform Sutra
lessons.mainIdea: The Platform Sutra tells the story of Huineng, honored in Chan as the Sixth Patriarch.
reading: The *Platform Sutra* is the only Chinese text given the title 'sutra' that centers on a Chinese teacher rather than the Buddha. It tells the story and sermons of *Huineng* (638–713), whom Chan honors as the Sixth Patriarch.

In the story, Huineng is a poor woodcutter who cannot read. He hears the Diamond Sutra recited and goes to a monastery. There he writes (through a helper) a short verse that shows, the text says, deeper insight than the head monk's. The master secretly passes the robe to him.

Scholars have found that the text was edited over time and that parts of the story reflect later disputes between Chan groups. Chan and Zen Buddhists still read it as a key text on sudden *awakening*.

words.d: a Chan text about the life and teaching of Huineng
Chinese Chan master (638–713) honored as the Sixth Patriarch
the insight Buddhists seek; in Chan, often called sudden

look.title: Two Verses on a Wall
look.text: The head monk writes that the body is like the Bodhi tree and the mind like a mirror stand, to be wiped clean so no dust can gather. Huineng answers that there is no tree and no stand; since all is empty from the start, where could dust land?
look.cite: Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the verse contest (Dunhuang version); see Philip Yampolsky, The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (1967)
look.prompt: How are the two verses different? Which idea from the Heart Sutra does Huineng's verse echo?

check.q: Who is the Platform Sutra about?
check.why: It tells Huineng's story and sermons.

check.q: What was Huineng's work before he became a monk, in the story?
choices: A merchant on the Silk Road
check.why: The text calls him a poor, unlettered woodcutter.

check.q: What have scholars found about the Platform Sutra?
choices: It is the oldest Buddhist text
check.why: The text changed across versions and reflects later disputes.

lessons.title: Koans and the Gateless Gate
lessons.mainIdea: A koan is a puzzling story or question that Zen teachers use in training; the Gateless Gate (1228) collects 48 of them.
reading: A *koan* is a short story, question or saying from a Chan master that a student works on in meditation. Teachers say a koan cannot be solved by logic alone. The student may work on one koan for months or years.

The *Gateless Gate* (Chinese Wumenguan, Japanese Mumonkan), compiled by Wumen Huikai in 1228, collects 48 koans with comments and verses. Its first case asks whether a dog has Buddha-nature. The master Zhaozhou answers, 'Wu!' (Japanese: Mu), 'No' or 'Not'.
The famous question 'What is the sound of one hand?' is not in the Gateless Gate. It comes from the Japanese Zen master Hakuin (1686–1769). Rinzai Zen teachers still use koans with students today.

words.d: a puzzling story or question used in Zen training
a collection of 48 koans compiled by Wumen in 1228 (Mumonkan)
the Mahayana teaching that all beings have the potential for buddhahood

look.title: Case One: Zhaozhou's Dog
look.text: A monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha-nature. Zhaozhou answers: 'Wu.' Wumen comments that the student must take up this one word day and night.
look.cite: Wumen Huikai, Gateless Gate (Wumenguan, 1228), case 1; see Robert Aitken, The Gateless Barrier (1990)
look.prompt: Mahayana teaching says all beings have Buddha-nature. Why might Zhaozhou's answer puzzle a student?

check.q: What is a koan?
choices: A puzzling story or question used in Zen training
check.why: Koans are worked on in Zen practice.

check.q: When was the Gateless Gate compiled?
check.why: Wumen compiled it in 1228.

check.q: Who is the source of 'the sound of one hand'?
check.why: The question comes from Hakuin, not the Gateless Gate.

lessons.title: Dogen and Just Sitting
lessons.mainIdea: Dogen founded Soto Zen in Japan and wrote the Shobogenzo, stressing seated meditation.
reading: *Dogen* (1200–1253) was a Japanese monk who traveled to China to study Chan. He returned and founded what became the Soto school of Zen in Japan. He was a monk of the Tendai school before he turned to Zen.
Dogen taught *zazen*, seated meditation, as the heart of practice. He described 'just sitting' (shikantaza), not as a means to reach awakening later but as the expression of awakening itself.

His major work, the *Shobogenzo* ('Treasury of the True Dharma Eye'), is a collection of essays in Japanese. It is famous for its poetic and difficult language. Soto Zen, one of Japan's largest schools, reads it closely today.

seated meditation in Zen
'Treasury of the True Dharma Eye', Dogen's collection of essays

lessons.title: Zen and Popular 'Zen'
lessons.mainIdea: Zen is a Buddhist tradition with monks, rules and texts; the popular word 'zen' often means only 'calm'.
reading: In English, 'zen' is often used as an ad word. A spa, a phone app or a tidy room may be called 'zen'. In this use, the word usually just means calm or simple. The word has drifted far from its Buddhist home.

Zen as a Buddhist tradition is much more. It has temples, *monastic* training, strict schedules, ordination, chanting, koans, sutras, precepts and teachers linked in lineages that trace back to the Buddha, as the tradition tells it.

Scholars and Zen teachers point out that borrowing the word without its setting can make the tradition hard to see. This is part of a wider discussion about *cultural appropriation*: using parts of another culture without understanding or respect.

words.d: having to do with monks and nuns and their way of life
using parts of another culture without understanding or respect
a line of teachers passing a tradition from one to the next

lessons.title: Kangyur and Tengyur
lessons.mainIdea: The Tibetan canon has two parts: the Kangyur, words of the Buddha, and the Tengyur, commentaries.
reading: Tibetan scholars translated a vast number of Indian Buddhist texts from Sanskrit into Tibetan, mostly between the 8th and 14th centuries. The collection was organized into two great parts by the scholar Buton (1290–1364) and others.

The *Kangyur* ('translated words') holds texts Tibetans count as the Buddha's words, including sutras, Vinaya and tantras. Editions have about 100 to 108 volumes. The *Tengyur* ('translated treatises') holds commentaries by Indian masters, in about 220 volumes or more.

Because many Sanskrit originals were lost, the Tibetan translations are often the only surviving versions. Scholars around the world use them. Tibetan monasteries honor the volumes as sacred and carry them in *procession* on special days.

words.d: the Tibetan collection of the Buddha's words
the Tibetan collection of Indian commentaries
a line of people moving together in a ceremony

lessons.title: Milarepa's Songs
lessons.mainIdea: Milarepa, a Tibetan yogi, is loved for his life story and his songs of realization.
reading: *Milarepa* (c. 1040–1123, dates vary) is one of Tibet's most beloved figures. His biography, written in the 15th century by Tsangnyon Heruka, tells that as a young man he used black magic to take revenge on relatives who had cheated his family, causing deaths.

Filled with regret, he sought the teacher Marpa. Marpa put him through years of hard labor, building and tearing down towers, before teaching him. Milarepa then meditated for years in mountain caves, the story says, living on nettles until his skin turned green.

His *songs*, collected in the Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa, express his insights in simple, vivid poems. Tibetan Buddhists see his life as proof that anyone, even someone who did great harm, can change. His teaching line is the Kagyu school.

words.d: a Tibetan yogi and poet (c. 1040–1123) famous for his life story and songs
in Tibetan Buddhism, poems of realization sung by teachers
a person devoted to meditation practice

look.title: From Harm to Healing

check.why: Marpa tested him with years of labor.

check.q: What do Tibetan Buddhists see in Milarepa's life?

check.why: His story shows transformation after wrongdoing.

lessons.title: The 'Tibetan Book of the Dead'
lessons.mainIdea: The Bardo Thodol is read to guide the dying and the dead, and its English title shaped how the West saw it.
reading: The *Bardo Thodol*, 'Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State', is part of a group of texts Tibetan tradition says was hidden by Padmasambhava and found in the 14th century by Karma Lingpa. A *bardo* is an in-between state, such as the time between death and rebirth.
In Tibet, a lama or relative reads the text aloud near a dying or recently dead person. Tibetan Buddhists believe it guides the person's mind through the bardo toward liberation or a good rebirth.

In 1927, W.Y. Evans-Wentz published an English version titled *The Tibetan Book of the Dead*. The title echoed the Egyptian Book of the Dead and made the text famous in the West. Some scholars note that it was only one of many funeral texts in Tibet and was read through Western ideas.

words.d: a Tibetan text read to guide the dying and dead through the bardo
an in-between state, such as the time between death and rebirth
how a text is received and understood by new readers

lessons.title: Shantideva's Guide
lessons.mainIdea: Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara is a poem on the bodhisattva path, deeply loved in Tibetan Buddhism.
reading: *Shantideva* was an Indian monk of the 8th century CE at Nalanda. His poem, the *Bodhicaryavatara* ('Entering the Path of Awakening'), describes the path of the bodhisattva in ten chapters.

The poem covers generosity, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom. Its chapter on patience is famous for looking at anger closely and giving reasons to let it go. It also includes verses dedicating all merit to the good of others.

Tibetan teachers, including the current Dalai Lama, often teach from this poem. The Dalai Lama has often quoted a dedication verse from its last chapter as a personal favorite. It shows how Indian texts live on through Tibetan *commentary*.
